facts.statement: Titanohierax gloveralleni, known as the Bahama eagle, was a large extinct hawk that lived during the Late Quaternary in the Caribbean.
facts.quote: Titanohierax gloveralleni, also known as the Bahama eagle, is a large species of extinct hawk from the Late Quaternary of the Caribbean.

facts.statement: Fossils of Titanohierax date back to the Pleistocene epoch.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Pleistocene

facts.statement: Remains of Titanohierax have been discovered on multiple islands within the Bahamas.
facts.quote: Remains of the animal have been found on multiple islands in the Bahamas.

facts.statement: The species is known from a limited collection of bones including a tarsometatarsus, a partial metacarpal, and a nearly complete right ulna.
facts.quote: The animal is known from a handful of bones found across multiple islands, including a tarsometatarsus, partial metacarpal, and nearly complete right ulna.

facts.statement: Alexander Wetmore described the species in 1937 based on a tarsometatarsus and a partial metacarpal.
facts.quote: The animal was described based on the former two by Alexander Wetmore in 1937

facts.statement: The first fossils were discovered in 1937 in cavern deposits on the island of Little Exuma in the Bahamas.
facts.quote: The first remains of Titanohierax were discovered in 1937 and were found in cavern deposits on Little Exuma, an island in The Bahamas.

facts.statement: Vivienne Knowles discovered the remains while separating them from cave earth intended for fertilizer.
facts.quote: The remains were found by Vivienne Knowles, who separated them from the cave earth that was to be used as fertilizer.

facts.statement: Alexander Wetmore described the species and named it Titanohierax gloveralleni in the same year the fossils were found.
facts.quote: The remains were described by Alexander Wetmore later in the same year, and he named one of the two extinct hawks as the new species Titanohierax gloveralleni.

facts.statement: Wetmore based the species diagnosis on a single tarsometatarsus that he compared to the great black hawk.
facts.quote: The species diagnosis was based on a single tarsometatarsus, which Wetmore noted to be similar to the great black hawk Buteogallus urubitinga

facts.statement: Wetmore initially misidentified the location of the fossils as Great Exuma instead of Little Exuma.
facts.quote: Wetmore mistakenly noted these fossils as coming from the island of Great Exuma

facts.statement: Max Hecht later identified the correct sites, noting that the fossiliferous soils had been removed.
facts.quote: Hecht noted sites matching the description given by Wetmore, with them having all their fossiliferous soils removed.

facts.statement: The holotype was likely found in Upper Pasture Cave on Little Exuma, located about fifty feet above sea level on the western side.
facts.quote: The remains of the holotype of Titanohierax were most likely found in the Upper Pasture Cave, which is located "about fifty feet above sea level facing the western side of Little Exuma".

facts.statement: Pierce Brodkorb provided the first confident dating of the avifauna including Titanohierax in 1959.
facts.quote: Pierce Brodkorb gives the first confident dating of the extinct Bahaman avifauna that Titanohierax was a part of in 1959

facts.statement: A sinkhole site known as Banana Hole was discovered in 1958 by Dr. J. C. Dickinson Jr. and excavated with Dr. Walter Auffenberg in August of that year.
facts.quote: The site, a sinkhole in limestone on the western side of the island, was found in 1958 by Dr. J. C. Dickinson Jr., who then carried out preliminary excavations together with Dr. Walter Auffenberg in August of the same year.

facts.statement: Geological and faunal evidence dated the Banana Hole site to the pre-Pamlico portion of the Wisconsin glacial stage, approximately 17,000 years old.
facts.quote: Based on a number of lines of evidence both geological and faunal, the age of the site was estimated to the Wisconsin glacial stage, specifically the pre-Pamlico portion. This puts the age of the site at around 17.000 years old.

facts.statement: During the Pleistocene, Titanohierax gloveralleni was an apex predator in the Bahamas that fed on large hutias like Geocapromys.
facts.quote: During the Pleistocene, T. gloveralleni would have been an apex predator of the Bahamian islands, feeding on animals including the large hutia Geocapromys.

facts.statement: Researchers believe habitat loss for the hawk and its prey, combined with potential human pressure, caused its extinction.
facts.quote: It is thought that a decline in suitable habitat for both it and its preferred prey items, along with possible pressure from human activity, would have led to the decline and eventual extinction of the animal.

facts.statement: In 1959, Brodkorb hypothesized that the accumulation of bones at Banana Hole was caused by a large raptor.
facts.quote: Brodkorb had noted in 1959 that the accumulation of remains at the Banana Hole site must have been caused by the activity of a large raptor

facts.statement: Olson and colleagues referred the ulnae to Titanohierax primarily based on their large size.
facts.quote: The referral was made mostly based on the large size of the specimens.

facts.statement: Referrals of fossils from New Providence and Hispaniola extended the known geographic range of Titanohierax.
facts.quote: These referrals would extend the known range of Titanohierax to the islands of New Providence and Hispaniola.

facts.statement: Notes by Bryan Patterson suggested that Aquila borrasi was actually Titanohierax borrasi, leading to a new combination.
facts.quote: However, notes from Arredondo's late collaborator Bryan Patterson would reveal that he already had the suspicion that these remains were of a species of Titanohierax, leading to the new combination Titanohierax borrasi.

facts.statement: In 2004, William Suárez refuted the assignment of Aquila borrasi to Titanohierax, concluding it was a valid species but belonged to a different genus.
facts.quote: In 2004, William Suárez published a paper that would refute the referral of Aquila borrasi to Titanohierax, based on new well-preserved material, establishing that even though borrasi was a valid species, it did not belong to the genus Titanohierax.

facts.statement: Suárez's work significantly reduced the known range of Titanohierax by removing all Cuban material from its classification.
facts.quote: This reduced the range of the animal considerably, with no Cuban material being referred to it any longer.

facts.statement: Titanohierax was a large hawk weighing approximately 7.3 kg, similar in size to female modern eagles.
facts.quote: Titanohierax was a very large hawk, with an estimated weight of around 7.3 kg, making it roughly equal in size to the females of the largest living eagles.

facts.statement: The only known fossils of Titanohierax are a tarsometatarsus, a partial metacarpal, and two ulnae.
facts.quote: The animal is solely known from a tarsometatarsus, partial metacarpal, and two ulnae.

facts.statement: A specimen of the ulna from the Florida State Museum measures 210 mm in length and 10 mm at its widest point.
facts.quote: The ulna of the animal was also of a considerable size, with the total length of a specimen from the Florida State Museum having been estimated at 210 mm long and 10 mm wide at its broadest extent.

facts.statement: Titanohierax was a giant hawk with a front claw measuring 57 mm and an estimated weight of 7.3 kg.
facts.quote: Titanohierax era un gavilán gigante cuya garra delantera llegaba a una longitud de 57 milímetros y a un peso estimado de cerca de 7.3 kilogramos

facts.statement: Titanohierax was slightly smaller than the largest known bird of prey, the Haast's eagle.
facts.quote: solo un poco menor que la mayor ave de presa conocida, el águila de Haast.

facts.statement: During the Pleistocene, Titanohierax served as an apex predator on the Bahaman islands.
facts.quote: During the Pleistocene, Titanohierax was an apex predator on the Bahaman islands.

facts.statement: 17,000 years ago, when Titanohierax lived, the Bahamas consisted of five major islands and several minor ones linked by lower sea levels.
facts.quote: When Titanohierax was alive 17.000 years ago, the Bahamas were much different from how they are today.

facts.statement: During the Wisconsinan glacial stage, temperatures on the islands were up to 4 degrees Celsius lower than today.
facts.quote: During this time, also referred to as the Wisconsinan glacial stage, the temperature on the islands would have been lower than today, with estimates suggesting a decrease of up to 4 degrees Celsius.

facts.statement: Titanohierax lived from the Late Pleistocene to the Holocene, between 0.129 and 0 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Late Pleistocene to Holocene (0.129 to 0 million years ago)

facts.statement: Wetmore described Titanohierax in 1937, comparing it to Buteogallus urubitinga.
facts.quote: Wetmore's 1937 description of the animal directly compares it to Buteogallus urubitinga

facts.statement: The genus Titanohierax was established by Wetmore in 1937.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Wetmore, 1937

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Titanohierax is Titanohierax gloveralleni.
facts.quote: type_species: Titanohierax gloveralleni

facts.statement: The closest living relatives of Titanohierax gloveralleni are modern species of the genus Buteogallus.
facts.quote: Los parientes vivos más cercanos de T. gloveralleni son las especies modernas de buteos del género Buteogallus.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the extinction of Titanohierax may be linked to a decline in its preferred prey, the rodent Geocapromys.
facts.quote: Olson and colleagues would go on to note that the extinction of Titanohierax and other large raptors from the West Indies was likely linked to a decline in the presence of the rodent Geocapromys, which is assumed to have been a preferred prey item.

facts.statement: A 2018 publication by Oswald and Steadman cites the loss of preferred habitat as a possible factor in Titanohierax's extinction.
facts.quote: Jessica Oswald and Steadman corroborate this in a 2018 publication, listing the loss of preferred habitat as another possible factor in the decline and eventual extinction of the animal.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the post-glacial decrease in Caribbean island size substantially contributed to Titanohierax's extinction, with some researchers arguing it did not.
facts.quote: They go on to mention that the decrease in size of the Caribbean islands following the end of the last glaciation event probably did not play a substantial part in their extinction.

facts.statement: The extinct Buteogallus borrasi was formerly classified within the genus Titanohierax alongside T. gloveralleni.
facts.quote: El extinto buteo Buteogallus borrasi fue anteriormente clasificado en este género junto a T. gloveralleni.

facts.statement: The tarsometatarsus of Titanohierax is significantly larger than that of any living buteogalline, its closest relatives.
facts.quote: Titanohieraxs tarsometatarsus is much larger than that of any living buteogalline, which are its closest relatives.

facts.statement: Wetmore identified a partial metacarpal as belonging to Titanohierax based on its similarity to Buteogallus urubitinga and its massive size.
facts.quote: Wetmore also described a partial metacarpal, which he referred to the species based on its similarity to B. urubitinga, and its massive size.

facts.statement: Titanohierax is an extinct genus of hawk that inhabited Cuba, Hispaniola, and the Bahamas.
facts.quote: Titanohierax es un género extinto de gavilán que habitó en Cuba, La Española y las Bahamas.

rejected.statement: A 1982 publication by Storrs Olson and colleagues tentatively assigned a nearly complete right ulna and a left ulna fragment from Banana Hole to Titanohierax.
rejected.quote: which tentatively attributed a nearly complete right ulna and a fragment of a left ulna from the site to Titanohierax.

rejected.statement: A 2019 study by David Steadman and colleagues argued that material from Hispaniola was too long and gracile to belong to T. gloveralleni.
rejected.quote: A 2019 paper by David Steadman and colleagues listed the referred material from Hispaniola as being much too long and gracile to belong to T. gloveralleni.
